overview: Abelisaurus comahuensis is the namesake of Abelisauridae, the dominant predator family of Gondwana in the Late Cretaceous. Known only from a skull — described by Bonaparte and Novas in 1985 from the Anacleto Formation of Patagonia (~83–80 Ma) — it establishes the basic anatomy of the abelisaurid skull: a tall, rough-surfaced cranium with large fenestrae, a short deep profile and small teeth.

Though fragmentary compared to Carnotaurus, Abelisaurus is historically important as the taxon that anchors the family name. Its skull surface texture — rugose and pitted rather than smooth — is now known to be characteristic of abelisaurids generally and supports the inference of extensive keratinous skull covering in these animals.

fossilSites.name: Anacleto Formation
fossilSites.note: Late Cretaceous (Campanian) continental deposits with the only known Abelisaurus skull.

articles.title: Discovery and significance
articles.body: José Bonaparte and Fernando Novas described Abelisaurus comahuensis in 1985, the same year as Carnotaurus. The skull — about 85 cm long — is the sole known element but shows enough anatomy to establish its abelisaurid affinities and distinguish it from Carnotaurus. Its discovery confirmed that the South American Late Cretaceous hosted a diverse abelisaurid fauna.

articles.title: Skull morphology
articles.body: The skull is tall and short compared to allosauroids of similar size. Large antorbital and infratemporal fenestrae reduce weight. The outer surface is roughened and pitted — now recognised as a taxonomic feature of abelisaurids generally, probably supporting a keratinous rhamphotheca (beak sheath) over parts of the skull. The dentition is small relative to skull size.

articles.title: Gondwanan abelisaurid radiation
articles.body: Abelisauridae radiated across the southern continents during the Cretaceous. South America, Africa, Madagascar and India all yield abelisaurid remains, demonstrating that this lineage was the dominant large theropod clade of Gondwana in the Cretaceous, analogous to the tyrannosaurs of Laurasia.

fossilRecord.formations: Anacleto Formation, Río Negro Province, Argentina
fossilRecord.material: A single partial skull without lower jaws.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Cretaceous Patagonian terrestrial ecosystems with titanosaur sauropods and abelisaurid predators.
fossilRecord.evidence: The skull alone was distinctive enough to diagnose the Abelisauridae family — its deep proportions and surface texture are diagnostic.

record.description: Abelisaurus comahuensis was a large abelisaurid theropod from the Anacleto Formation of Patagonia. The genus is based on a single incomplete skull; no confidently associated postcranial skeleton is known.
facts: The holotype is a partial skull lacking much of the snout and lower jaws.
Its body proportions, size and external covering must largely be inferred from other abelisaurids.

review.ageReviewNote: The Anacleto Formation is generally dated to the early Campanian.
